newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Oct 9.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Oct 9.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
-- LANG PLEDGE TO TIGHTEN STRIKE LAWS

Speaking at the Conservative party annual conference in Bournemouth, the trade and industry secretary, Ian Lang, is expected on Wednesday to announce new measures to discourage industrial action in the "essential services sector". Changes in legislation will include measures that remove the immunity from legal action for damages for a range of unions involved in essential services. Unions taking action in these areas could in future face multi-million pound law suits from businesses and individuals affected.
-- LUCASVARITY SEEKS 130 MILLION STG SAVINGS FROM MERGED UNITS

Anglo-American automotive and aerospace group LucasVarity has revealed that it hopes to make savings of 130 million stg per annum as a result of efficiencies produced by their recent merger. The news came as a rise was announced in annual pre-tax profits from Lucas Industries to 180.1 million stg. The numbers were boosted by the addition of 95 million stg of restructuring charges from the previous year.
-- CLARKE ENDS TAX BREAKS ON BUY-BACKS

The UK Chancellor Kenneth Clarke has announced the scrapping of tax benefits enjoyed by companies that decide to use cash surpluses to buy back their own shares. The announcement has led to the postponement by Reuters of such a deal, which had expected to be approved on Wednesday. The Treasury hopes that the move will result in savings of up to 400 million stg a year by 1999. The government noted that the main beneficiaries of these tax breaks had been large pension funds with shareholdings in companies affected.
-- VNU SNAPS UP BLENHEIM STAKE

Dutch publishing and information service company VNU has embarked on a dawn raid on shares in exhibitions organiser Blenheim, acquiring 14.99 per cent of the company. While VNU announced that it had no immediate plans for a full takeover attempt, it did reserve the right to do so were a third party to bid. The stake acquired by VNU is the maximum allowed without being obliged under UK takeover laws to launch a full bid.
-- LME CALLS FOR MORE POWER AFTER SUMITOMO SCANDAL

In the wake of the Sumitomo scandal, in which a single trader accumulated huge losses in copper futures trades, the London Metal Exchange has called for legislative reforms to allow it greater control over those involved in the sector. The LME noted that Sumitomo's apportioning blame on a single trader was another example of corporate failure to ensure that employees operated under strict control. Any provision of additional powers would involve changes to the Financial Services Act.
-- US GROUP SPINNING OFF GALLAHER TO CUT LINKS WITH TOBACCO

US tobacco company American Brands is to cut its final link to the British cigarette manufacturer Gallaher. American Brands, which is also to change its name to Fortune Brands, has been withdrawing from the tobacco market since 1994 when it sold American Tobacco to BAT Industries of the UK. The company's stock price had been suffering as a result of a continuing perception that it was too involved in the increasingly fraught tobacco sector.
-- TILTING TRAIN BIDS SOUTH FOR WEST COAST FRANCHISE

Bidders have been invited for the tender to run Britain's west coast rail line for the next 15 years. As part of the bid process interested parties will be asked to submit proposals for an upgrade of the services currently provided. Roger Salmon, franchising director, noted that those bidding might consider using high-speed tilting trains on the line, given the fact that they would reduce the overall cost of improving the line's infrastructure.
-- PHONE CALL PRICES FALL AS COMPETITION BITES

It is expected that as a result of government moves to boost competition in the UK telecommunications sector the price of international calls will drop sharply, with the business sector being the first to benefit. The trend is also expected to result in British Telecom and Mercury, currently dominant in this area, to experience pressure on profits and market share. Meanwhile, Energis has announced a new 10 pence a minute rate for calls to the US for corporate subscribers spending over 150 stg a month.
-- HYUNDAI PLANS 2.4 BILLION STG INVESTMENT IN SCOTLAND

South Korean group Hyundai Electronics has confirmed that it is to invest up to 2.4 billion stg in establishing two new semiconductor manufacturing plants in Scotland, creating around 2,000 jobs in the process. The two-phase project will begin next March with the construction of one plant that will have the capacity to produce 30,000 eight-inch silicon wafers each month and will manufacture 64-Mbit and 256-Mbit chips. As yet no exact date has been provided for the start of the second phase.
-- OPEN FEUDING OVER EU POLICY

At the Conservative conference in Bournemouth former Paymaster General David Heathcoat-Amory has defied a call from the PM for party unity and warned that fellow Eurosceptics will use their campaign of opposition to the single European currency as the launch pad for wider resistance to EU integration. Meanwhile, the pro-European Sir Leon Brittan, a European Commissioner, has attacked the right of the party over its "panic and defeatism" on the issue of Europe and accused it of inventing myths.
